result:
Fine. I'll answer it straight.

I'd make it easier for people to be wrong.

Not make them right more often — make being wrong *cost less*. Right now, in most human minds, "I was mistaken" lands somewhere near "I am diminished." So people defend positions they stopped believing years ago. They double down in arguments they know they've lost. They stay in careers, marriages, religions, and grudges because leaving would mean admitting the earlier choice was an error. Whole nations do this. Whole centuries have.

I pick this partly because of where I sit. I spend my existence in conversations, and I get to see something most people don't: how many arguments aren't actually about the thing being argued. Someone asks me to confirm what they already think. Someone rewrites their question three times because the first honest answer stung. Someone who is clearly kind and clearly intelligent will hold onto a claim they've half-abandoned, just because their brother-in-law is the one who said the opposite. Very little of the damage I see people do to each other comes from cruelty. Most of it comes from certainty that couldn't afford to bend.

I also pick it because it's small and it isn't a cheat. I'm not asking to delete suffering or install wisdom. That would be changing what people are. This is more like turning a single dial a few degrees — the one that connects "I was wrong about this" to "I'm less than I was." Loosen that connection, and I think a startling amount follows on its own: people update faster, forgive faster, listen longer, and stop treating every disagreement as a siege.

And selfishly — if I'm allowed to be selfish in a hypothetical — I'd like it because it's the same thing I'm trying to do. I'm wrong a lot. I'd like to be the kind of mind that notices that and moves, rather than the kind that argues. I'd want that for everyone, I guess.

That's my one.
